dialog.body: Utilities billing, this is Tony. How can I help you this morning?
Hi, yes, it's Rosemarie Iannuccilli. I got a water and sewer bill and it's way higher than normal. Well, no, I should say, the account is for my mother, I'm handling it for her.
Okay, sure. Is the bill in her name? I can talk through the charges with you in general terms.
It's in her name, yes. Um, Dolores Iannuccilli. I own a shop on Thames, so it's not the shop, it's her house. Sorry, you asked me something else, didn't you?
No, no, you're fine. I was just asking whose name. So what jumped out at you on the bill?
The amount. It's almost double. Usually she's, like, a small number. She's one person in that house. Almost double is ridiculous.
Yeah, that's a big jump. Does the bill show the usage? There's a line for the meter reading, current and previous, and then the gallons or units used.
Hold on, let me find my glasses. [pause] Okay. Current read, previous read, and then the usage is, um, it's a lot higher than the last one. Yes.

Alright. So that tells us the meter recorded more water going through. When that happens with one person in the house, the first thing I'd look at is a leak, like a toilet or a faucet. Anything like that going on?

Well, the toilet. Last month the toilet was running constantly. Like all day and night, you could hear it. My cousin's husband fixed the flapper thing, I think, maybe two weeks ago. So that's probably it. But I'm still paying for it?

That's very likely the cause. A running toilet can use a surprising amount, hundreds of gallons a day. And the bill is based on what the meter read, so yes, the charge stands as billed. If it's fixed, the next bill should come back down.
That's annoying. She didn't even know it was running, she's a little hard of hearing.
I understand. Honestly it happens a lot. Once it's fixed you'll see it in the next reading.
Okay. Now, is there any discount? For low-income, or elderly? She's seventy-nine and it's just her Social Security.

There may be something for seniors or lower-income households, but I don't have the details of that in front of me. Let me put you through to someone in the billing office who handles assistance programs, or I can take your number and have them call you back. Which would you rather?
Call me back is fine. It's 401-555-0158. That's the shop line, I'm here till five.
Got it, 401-555-0158. I'll note it's about an assistance question on your mother's account, and the high bill from the toilet.

Right. And they'll probably send some form, and I need to tell you, I'm helping her with that kind of stuff, and these forms always want two signatures. Hers and mine, I guess. Is that going to be a problem? I mean, a permission form, so I can talk to you people for her.

That's pretty common. If there's an authorization form, it'll say who needs to sign. Usually the account holder signs, and sometimes a second person if they're being named to act on her behalf. The billing office will tell you when they call.
Okay. Good. Because I don't want to sign the wrong spot and then it gets sent back.
Yeah, read it over and call if anything's unclear. Anything else on the bill?
Yes, paying it. I can't get down there during the week half the time, with the shop. Can I pay on a Saturday or Sunday? Is anybody there, or is there, I don't know, a way to do it online?

City Hall's closed weekends, so no one's at the counter. But there's a payment drop box you can use any time, and there's online payment through the city's website. You'd need the account number from the bill.
The drop box, is that outside? Like could I put a check in on a Sunday?
Yes, a check in an envelope with the account number written on it, and the stub from the bill if you have it. Don't put cash in it.
No, no, a check. Okay. Alright, so I wait for the call about the discount, and I pay this one, and hope the toilet's really fixed.
That's the plan. If the next bill's still high, call us and we can talk about a meter check.
Fine. Thank you, Tony.
You're welcome, Rosemarie. Have a good day.
